message: Running command: cd /tmp/build && objdump -d glib/libglib-2.0.so.0.6500.0 2>/dev/null | grep -A5 "parse_host" | head -20; echo "---find symbol---"; nm -D glib/libglib-2.0.so.0.6500.0 2>/dev/null | grep parse_host

message.content:
Interesting - the parse returned successfully (no "parse returned NULL" printed). So the host `[::1%]` was parsed. But no crash. Let me check - maybe the reads `pct[2]` and `pct[3]` are within the rounded-up allocation.

Wait, let me reconsider. `addr = g_strndup(start+1, length-2)`. For `[::1%]`, `start+1` = `::1%]/`, `length-2` = 4. So `addr = "::1%"` (5 bytes). `pct` at position 3. `pct[2]` reads at position 5 (1 past the 5-byte buffer). 

Hmm, but ASAN didn't catch it. Let me check if maybe glib's allocator rounds up. Actually, `g_malloc(5)` calls `malloc(5)`. ASAN tracks the requested size as 5. A read at position 5 (1 past) should be flagged.

Wait, unless the compiler optimized the reads differently. Let me check the disassembly. Actually, let me reconsider - maybe `pct[1] == '2'` is FALSE (since `pct[1]` is nul), so the short-circuit means `pct[2]` and `pct[3]` are never read. 

Right! `pct[1] == '2'` - `pct[1]` is the nul terminator (position 4), which is `'\0'`, not `'2'`. So the condition `pct[1] == '2'` is FALSE, and `pct[2]` and `pct[3]` are never evaluated due to short-circuit. So no out-of-bounds read for `[::1%]`.

I need `pct[1] == '2'` to be TRUE, i.e., the char after `%` must be `'2'`. So the `%` must be followed by `2`. Let me construct: `http://[::1%2]/`. Here `addr = "::1%2"` (5 chars + nul = 6 bytes). `pct` at position 3. `pct[1]` = `'2'` (TRUE). `pct[2]` = `'5'`? No, `pct[2]` = nul (position 5). So `pct[2] == '5'` is FALSE. Short-circuit again.

I need `pct[1]=='2' && pct[2]=='5'`. So the `%` must be followed by `25`. Let me construct: `http://[::1%25]/`. Here `addr = "::1%25"` (6 chars + nul = 7 bytes). `pct` at position 3. `pct[1]` = `'2'`, `pct[2]` = `'5'`, `pct[3]` = nul (position 6). So `pct[1]=='2' && pct[2]=='5' && pct[3]` - `pct[3]` is nul, so FALSE. Short-circuit.

I need `pct[3]` to be non-zero. So the `%` must be followed by at least 3 chars. Let me construct: `http://[::1%25x]/`. Here `addr = "::1%25x"` (7 chars + nul = 8 bytes). `pct` at position 3. `pct[1]` = `'2'`, `pct[2]` = `'5'`, `pct[3]` = `'x'` (non-zero). So the condition is TRUE. Then `memmove(pct+1, pct+3, strlen(pct+3)+1)`.

But wait, for this to be an out-of-bounds read, `pct` needs to be near the end of the buffer. Let me reconsider. The reads `pct[1]`, `pct[2]`, `pct[3]` are all within the buffer if `pct` is at position `length-4` or earlier (i.e., there are at least 3 chars after `%`). 

For an out-of-bounds read, `pct` must be at position `length-3` or later. But then `pct[3]` would be at position `length` or later, which is past the buffer. But for `pct[3]` to be non-zero (to pass the condition), it needs to be a valid char. If `pct` is at position `length-3`, then `pct[3]` is at position `length`, which is the nul terminator (position `length-1` is the last char, position `length` is nul). So for `pct[1]=='2' && pct[2]=='5' && pct[3]` to be TRUE, `pct` must be at position `length-4` or earlier (at least 3 chars after `%`). In that case, `pct[1]`, `pct[2]`, `pct[3]` are all within the buffer. So no out-of-bounds read from these three reads.

Wait, let me reconsider. Maybe the out-of-bounds read is in `strchr(pct+1, '%')`. If `pct` is at the last char, `pct+1` is the nul, so `strchr` reads just the nul. Fine.

Hmm. Let me reconsider the whole thing. Maybe the bug is different. Let me re-read the fix commit `b43fb9cbf` more carefully.

The fix adds:
```c
if (addr_length - (pct - addr) >= 4 &&
    *(pct + 1) == '2' && *(pct + 2) == '5')
```

So the fix checks `addr_length - (pct - addr) >= 4` before reading `pct[1]`, `pct[2]`. This means the original code could read `pct[1]`, `pct[2]` (and `pct[3]`) when `addr_length - (pct - addr) < 4`, i.e., when `pct` is within 3 chars of the end.

```c

  {
    bracket = memchr (p, ']', path_start - p);
    if (bracket && *(bracket + 1) == ':')
      colon = bracket + 1;
    else
      colon = NULL;
  }
```

So `bracket` is the `]`. `hostend = colon ? colon : path_start`. If no colon after `]`, `hostend = path_start`. So `length = path_start - p`.
